title: Tailbone pain, explained in pictures
summary: A visual guide to coccydynia. Why sitting loads the tailbone, how it gets injured, how to tell it from other pain, what sitting and standing X-rays show, and how treatment is stepped up.
text: Tailbone pain (coccydynia) makes much more sense once you can see what is happening. This guide walks through it in pictures, one step at a time (moving diagrams and slides), with links to the full articles if you want to go deeper. Key points - When you sit, your weight rests on two sitting bones . Leaning back or slouching adds the coccyx as a third point , and that is when it hurts. - The coccyx is a small anchor for the pelvic floor muscles, the buttock muscle and several ligaments , so it is never just "a leftover bone". - Pain usually comes from a fall, childbirth or repeated strain such as long sitting or riding over bumps. - True coccydynia is pain you can point to with one finger , worst when sitting and when getting up . - Sitting and standing X-rays compared side by side can show a coccyx that bends too far or slips. In one large study they found a likely cause in about 7 in 10 people. - About 9 in 10 people get better without surgery. 1. A small bone with a big job The coccyx is made of three to five small segments at the very bottom of the spine, joined to the sacrum above it. It is small, but it is an anchor point. The pelvic floor muscles that support the bladder and bowel attach to it, as do fibres of the large buttock muscle (gluteus maximus) and strong ligaments that tie it to the pelvis. That is why tailbone pain is often more than a bone problem. Tight or overworked pelvic floor muscles can pull on the coccyx, and a painful coccyx can make those muscles tense up in turn. 2. Why sitting hurts: the tripod Sit up straight and your weight rests on the two sitting bones (the ischial tuberosities), with the coccyx held clear of the seat. Lean back, slouch or sink into a soft sofa, and the pelvis rolls backwards. Now the coccyx becomes the third leg of a tripod, and it is not built to carry that load. This is why the simplest advice works so often: sit tall or lean slightly forward, and use a cushion with a gap at the back. Read more: 8 ways to sit more comfortably with tailbone pain 3. Not every coccyx is the same shape Some coccyges curve gently, others hook sharply forward, and in some the joint is already slightly out of line. Shape alone doesn't cause pain, but it changes how pressure is spread when you sit, so some people are more likely to develop problems. Read more: Why some tailbones hurt and others don't 4. How the coccyx gets hurt Route Examples What tends to happen A sudden blow from outside A fall onto the bottom on stairs, a wet floor or ice; a hard landing on a ride or water slide Bruising, a sprain of the joint, a fracture or a joint that slips out of line Pressure from inside Childbirth, especially a difficult or assisted delivery The coccyx is pushed backwards and the joint and ligaments are strained Repeated strain Long hours sitting, especially slouched; two-wheeler riding over bumps; cycling or rowing Small, repeated overload that builds up without a single injury Body weight at either end Higher weight changes how the pelvis tilts when sitting; very low weight leaves little padding Either can increase the load on the coccyx Common ways the coccyx is injured. Sometimes no single cause can be found. Read more: Tailbone pain after having a baby · Two-wheelers, potholes and tailbone pain · Does body weight affect tailbone pain? 5. Recognising it True coccydynia has a clear pattern: - Pain right at the base of the spine, in the midline, that you can point to with one finger. - Worse when sitting, especially leaning back, and often a sharp jab when getting up from a chair. - Sometimes worse when opening the bowels or during intercourse, because the coccyx sits close to the back passage. Pain mainly in one buttock, pain shooting down the leg, or numbness and tingling usually point somewhere else. 6. Is it really the coccyx? Coccydynia Pelvic floor muscle pain Pain from the lower back Where The tip of the tailbone, in the midline Deeper and more spread out; pressure in the back passage or vagina Lower back, often spreading into the buttock or down the leg Set off by Sitting, leaning back, getting up Stress, bladder or bowel problems, long sitting Bending, lifting, long standing or sitting Nerve signs None None Sometimes tingling, numbness or weakness in the leg What helps Taking pressure off the coccyx; hands-on treatment of the joint Relaxing and releasing the pelvic floor muscles Treatment directed at the spine Three common sources of pain low in the back, and how they usually differ. A careful examination tells them apart; they can also occur together. A few less common conditions can feel similar, and some need other treatment. If you have fever, bleeding from the back passage, pain that is constant even at rest or at night, or unexplained weight loss, see a doctor promptly. Read more: Pain near the tailbone that isn't coming from the coccyx · When tailbone pain needs urgent attention 7. Seeing the problem: sitting and standing X-rays An ordinary X-ray is taken lying down or standing, when no weight is on the coccyx, so it often looks normal. The French physician Jean-Yves Maigne developed a simple comparison: one side-on X-ray standing and one sitting. Comparing the two shows how the coccyx behaves under your weight. In Maigne's study of 208 people with coccydynia, the two pictures showed a likely cause in about 7 in 10. A coccyx that bent too far (hypermobile) and a joint that slipped backwards were the most common findings. Backward slips were more common in people with a higher body weight, and small bony spurs at the tip in slimmer people. Imaging is not needed for everyone. Most of the information comes from your history and a careful examination, and an X-ray is added when it will change the treatment. Read more: What happens at a coccydynia consultation 8. Which way has it moved? When the coccyx is out of line, the direction matters. A coccyx pushed inwards and one pushed outwards need different hands-on treatment, which is why it is checked before anything is done. Read more: A displaced tailbone: why the direction of the shift matters 9. Treatment, step by step Treatment starts with the simplest, safest steps and moves up only if needed: 1. Take the pressure off. Sit tall or lean slightly forward, take breaks, and use a wedge or U-shaped cushion with the gap at the back. 2. Hands-on treatment. Treatment of the coccyx joint and release of the tight muscles around it, by a clinician trained in coccyx problems, with exercises to keep it moving well. 3. Medicines for short-term relief, when your doctor advises them. 4. Injections or nerve blocks , such as a ganglion impar block, for pain that persists despite the earlier steps. 5. Surgery to remove the coccyx, kept for a small number of carefully selected people because of its real risk of wound problems. About 9 in 10 people improve with the first, non-surgical steps. Read more: How coccydynia is treated · Why "bone setting" can be dangerous Summary Tailbone pain is a mechanical problem with a clear pattern, and it can be worked out. Find out exactly where the pain comes from, take the load off the coccyx, treat the joint and the muscles around it, and step up only if needed. Most people get back to sitting comfortably without surgery.

title: Why "bone setting" for tailbone pain can be dangerous
summary: Pressing or massaging the tailbone from outside, without knowing which way it has shifted, can push an inward-displaced coccyx deeper into the pelvis. Dr Rajveer Singh explains the risk.
text: Many people with tailbone pain are taken to a local "bone setter" for an external massage or a quick push to put it back. Dr Rajveer Singh sees patients every month whose pain became worse afterwards. Here is why. Key points - A displaced coccyx can shift inward into the pelvis or outward . From the outside, you can't tell which. - If it has shifted inward, pressing on it from outside pushes it deeper into the pelvis : a small displacement becomes a bigger injury. - Treating a displaced coccyx without first checking the direction on a dynamic X-ray is unsafe, and in Dr Rajveer's view unethical. - A specialist realigns the coccyx with internal manipulation , aimed in the right direction. How a quick push can go wrong The coccyx sits at the very bottom of the spine, partly hidden inside the pelvis. When it has been pushed inward (an anterior subluxation), the part you can feel from outside is already further in than it should be. Pressing on it from behind adds to the same force that displaced it. The muscles around it go into spasm, and sitting becomes even more painful. Before any treatment What it shows A careful history How it started: a fall, childbirth, long sitting, a sudden jolt An examination Where it hurts, how the coccyx and the pelvic floor muscles respond A dynamic X-ray (sitting and standing) Which way the coccyx has moved, and how much it moves when you sit What a specialist checks before treating a displaced coccyx. What safe treatment looks like Once the direction is known, the coccyx is realigned by internal manipulation, gently and from the right side, in a short series of sessions. Exercises chosen for your type of shift then help keep it in place. See tailbone subluxation: why the direction decides the treatment. If you've already had bone setting Don't worry, and don't repeat it. If the pain is the same or worse, book an assessment. Many patients still recover well once the direction of the shift is known and treated properly.

title: Kegel exercises can make tailbone pain worse
summary: Kegels and "butt-squeezing" are often suggested for pelvic pain. Dr Rajveer Singh explains why they can pull an inward-shifted or fractured coccyx further out of place, and what to do instead.
text: Kegel exercises are good for many people, especially after childbirth. But if your tailbone has been pushed inward , or it is fractured, squeezing exercises can do harm. Dr Rajveer Singh asks his patients to stop them until the direction of the problem is known. Key points - The pelvic floor muscles are attached to the coccyx. - If the coccyx has shifted inward (an anterior subluxation) or is fractured, contracting these muscles pulls it further inside. - So Kegels and "butt-squeezing" exercises should not be done until a specialist has checked which way the coccyx has moved. - The right exercises depend on the direction of the shift, and are taught after the coccyx has been realigned. Why squeezing can make it worse Several of the pelvic floor muscles, including the coccygeus and parts of the levator ani, attach to the coccyx. When they contract, they pull on it. With a normally placed coccyx that's fine. But if it has already been pushed into the pelvis, each squeeze tugs it further the wrong way. The displacement increases, the pain lasts longer, and treatment becomes harder. Exercise Coccyx in normal position Coccyx shifted inward or fractured Kegel / squeezing exercises Usually fine Avoid: they pull the coccyx further in What helps Exercises a physiotherapist teaches you Diagnosis first, internal manipulation, then direction-specific exercises Squeezing exercises and the coccyx, as Dr Rajveer Singh advises. What to do instead 1. Stop squeezing exercises if you have tailbone pain and haven't been examined yet. 2. Take the pressure off with a cut-out cushion and regular breaks from sitting (see sitting with tailbone pain). 3. Find out the direction. An examination and a dynamic X-ray show whether the coccyx has moved inward or outward (see tailbone subluxation). 4. Follow a plan made for you. Once the coccyx is back in line, your exercises are chosen for your particular shift. After childbirth New mothers are often told to start Kegels straight away. If you have tailbone pain after delivery, check with a specialist first: childbirth is one of the commonest causes of an inward-shifted coccyx (see tailbone pain after pregnancy).

title: A displaced tailbone: why the direction of the shift matters
summary: A displaced coccyx can be pushed inward into the pelvis or outward. Dr Rajveer Singh explains why the direction must be known first, how treatment differs, and how one patient recovered.
text: After a fall, a jolt or childbirth, the coccyx rarely breaks cleanly. More often it is pushed slightly out of line with the rest of the spine. This is called a subluxation , and it is one of the commonest reasons tailbone pain doesn't go away on its own. Key points - A subluxed coccyx shifts in one of two directions: inward into the pelvis (anterior) or outward (posterior). - The direction matters more than anything else, because the right treatment for one can make the other worse. - Dr Rajveer checks the direction on a dynamic X-ray (taken sitting and standing) before any manipulation or exercise programme. - Treatment then follows three steps: an exact diagnosis, internal manipulation to realign the coccyx, and exercises chosen for that direction. Inward or outward: what's the difference? What Inward shift (anterior) Outward shift (posterior) Where the coccyx goes Into the pelvis Backwards, towards the skin What makes it worse Pressure from outside, and squeezing the pelvic floor Direct pressure when sitting Never do Kegel or "butt-squeezing" exercises; external "bone setting" Long sitting on flat, hard seats Treatment Internal manipulation, then exercises for an inward shift Internal manipulation, then exercises for an outward shift The two directions of tailbone subluxation, as Dr Rajveer Singh explains them. Why the X-ray comes first From the outside, both kinds of subluxation can feel the same: pain on sitting, pain getting up, pain at the base of the spine. But they need opposite handling. A dynamic X-ray, taken sitting and standing, shows how the coccyx actually moves under your body weight. Dr Rajveer's rule is simple: no manipulation, no exercise programme and no physical therapy should begin without knowing the direction of the shift. The three steps of treatment 1. Diagnose exactly. The examination and a dynamic X-ray show whether the coccyx has shifted inward or outward, and by how much. 2. Realign. Internal manipulation gently moves the coccyx back into line. It is done in a short series of sessions, usually within about a week, spaced at the right intervals. 3. Keep it there. Exercises chosen for your direction of shift strengthen and relax the right muscles, so the coccyx stays in place. Doing them faithfully at home is what makes the result last. A patient's recovery When What happened Day 1 An IT professional from Pune, badly affected by tailbone pain, was diagnosed with an outward (posterior) subluxation on a dynamic X-ray Week 1 A short series of internal manipulation sessions corrected the outward shift Month 4 Marked recovery, after following the home exercise programme very closely Months 5 to 8 He continued the exercises for another 3 to 4 months to keep the coccyx stable One patient's recovery from an outward subluxation (shared by Dr Rajveer Singh). Not everyone recovers at the same pace, but the pattern is typical: the manipulation corrects the position, and the exercises keep it. What to avoid while it heals - Cycling and riding motorbikes, which put your weight on a narrow saddle right under the coccyx (see two-wheelers and tailbone pain). - Sitting flat on hard chairs without a cut-out cushion (see sitting with tailbone pain). - Bending forward without support. - Squeezing exercises if your coccyx has shifted inward (see Kegel exercises and tailbone pain). - External "bone setting" (see why bone setting can be dangerous). Treat it early Tailbone pain is often brushed off as soreness that will pass. When the coccyx is out of line, it usually doesn't. Left alone, sitting at work, driving and even sleeping can become harder over months. Early assessment and the right treatment are much easier than undoing years of strain.

title: How coccydynia is treated, and how often each treatment works
summary: Tailbone pain is treated in steps, from better sitting and hands-on care to injections and, rarely, surgery. What each step involves and the success rates reported in research.
text: Most people with tailbone pain get better without surgery. Treatment works like a ladder: start with the simplest, safest steps, and climb only if they don't help enough. Reviews put the success rate of the non-surgical steps at about 9 in 10 . Key points - About 90% of people with coccydynia improve with non-surgical care. - The first step is changing how and how long you sit : a wedge or cut-out cushion, leaning forward, and regular breaks. - Manipulation of the coccyx, usually combined with an injection, helped about 75–92% of patients in older clinical series. General physiotherapy (heat, ultrasound) helped little in the same studies, so the type of hands-on treatment matters. - Injections are an option when pain persists; reported relief varies widely between studies. - Surgery (coccygectomy) is kept for a small, carefully selected group, and has a real risk of wound infection. The steps at a glance Step What it involves What studies report 1. Sitting changes Wedge or U-shaped (cut-out) cushion, leaning forward, breaks every 20–30 minutes Recommended first-line in all reviews; a cut-out or wedge cushion is preferred over a doughnut ring (MSD Manual) 2. Hands-on treatment Internal or external manipulation of the coccyx, release of the pelvic floor muscles, stretching and exercises Manipulation with injection cured about 85% in a 120-patient trial (Wray 1991); other series report 75–92% improvement (Perkins, Ramsey, summarised by Garg and Ahuja). The same trial found general physiotherapy of little help 3. Medicines Short courses of anti-inflammatory pain relief, sometimes medicines for nerve pain Helpful for symptoms; not a cure on their own 4. Injections Local anaesthetic and steroid around the coccyx, or a ganglion impar block About 60% responded to steroid and anaesthetic injections (Wray 1991); ganglion impar block helped 6 of 8 patients at 6 months in a small CT-guided study (Datir 2010) 5. Ablation Radiofrequency treatment of the nerves or the ganglion impar Used for pain that keeps coming back after injections; evidence is from small studies 6. Surgery Removal of part or all of the coccyx (coccygectomy) Needed by almost 20% in Wray's trial, with over 90% success; 85–100% improvement in carefully selected patients across studies; complication rates of 0–50% across studies, mostly wound infection Coccydynia treatment options and reported results (Garg and Ahuja 2021, unless stated). These figures come from different studies with different patients and definitions of success, so they can't be compared directly. They do show a clear pattern: the simple steps help most people, and the risky steps are only for a few. Step 1: sitting differently Sitting puts weight on the coccyx, especially when you lean back. Small changes take that pressure off: - Lean forward slightly so your weight rests on your thigh bones and sitting bones, not on the tailbone. - Use a wedge or cut-out cushion with the gap at the back. A doughnut ring can still press on the coccyx. - Stand up every 20–30 minutes, and avoid low, soft sofas. See sitting with tailbone pain for more detail. Step 2: hands-on treatment This is the core of what we do at the clinic. After a careful examination, the clinician gently moves the coccyx back towards its normal position and range of movement, and releases the tight pelvic floor muscles that pull on it (see conditions linked to tailbone pain). Treatment is usually done from the inside, through the back passage, because that is the only way to reach the front of the coccyx and the muscles attached to it. It is explained fully before it starts, and you can stop at any time. People whose coccyx is too mobile or slightly displaced when they sit often respond well. Those whose coccyx is very stiff may need more sessions or another step. This is one reason we assess the coccyx shape and movement first. Step 3: medicines Anti-inflammatory tablets or gels can ease pain while other treatment takes effect. They are not a long-term answer, and should be taken only as advised by your doctor. Step 4: injections If pain persists for several weeks despite the steps above, an injection of local anaesthetic and steroid around the painful joint can calm it down. Another option is a ganglion impar block , an injection at a small nerve cluster in front of the coccyx. Injections should be done by a specialist under X-ray or CT guidance. Steps 5 and 6: ablation and surgery For the few people whose pain continues despite everything else, radiofrequency treatment of the nerves or removal of the coccyx may be considered. Surgery gives good results in carefully chosen patients, usually those with an unstable or clearly abnormal coccyx on sitting and standing X-rays. Because the wound is close to the back passage, infection is the main risk. Our approach We start at the bottom of the ladder, with a thorough history and examination, sitting advice and hands-on treatment, and refer on only when it is genuinely needed. Most of our patients need only a few sessions. Book a consultation in Delhi or online.

title: Tailbone pain in numbers
summary: How common is tailbone pain, who gets it, what causes it and how often treatment works: the key figures from medical research, each with its source.
text: Coccydynia (tailbone or coccyx pain) is one of the most under-studied causes of back pain. This page brings together the numbers that are actually backed by published research, explains what they mean, and is honest about what is still unknown. Key points - Nobody knows exactly how many people have coccydynia. It is thought to make up only around 1% of people seen for spine pain, but it is often missed or recorded as "low back pain". - Women are affected about five times as often as men. - Half or more of patients remember an injury such as a fall. Childbirth accounts for a smaller but important share in women. - Body weight matters at both ends: both a high and a very low body mass index (BMI) raise the risk. - About 9 in 10 people improve without surgery. The key figures at a glance Question What research reports Source How common is it? Exact incidence has not been reported; roughly 1% of people seen for musculoskeletal or spine pain Lirette 2014; BMJ Best Practice Women vs men About 5 women for every man Lirette 2014; Garg and Ahuja 2021 Who gets it Mostly adults and teenagers; uncommon in young children Lirette 2014 Remember an injury first 50–65% of patients Garg and Ahuja 2021 Linked to childbirth 7.3% of women's cases in one specialist clinic Maigne 2012 Abnormal coccyx movement when sitting About 69% of patients on sitting and standing X-rays Maigne 2000; Garg and Ahuja 2021 Bony spur at the tip About 14% of patients Garg and Ahuja 2021 Weight above which risk rises BMI over 27.4 in women, over 29.4 in men Garg and Ahuja 2021 Better without surgery About 90% Lirette 2014; Garg and Ahuja 2021 Coccydynia key figures. Full references are listed at the end of this article. Why the exact numbers are uncertain Coccydynia rarely gets its own diagnosis code. In many records it is grouped with general low back pain, and many people never see a doctor about it, often out of embarrassment. That is why the reviews we rely on say plainly that its true incidence is unknown. Be wary of any website quoting a precise share of the population: we could not find a reliable source for such figures. Who is more likely to get it? - Women, partly because of the shape of the pelvis and because of childbirth. See why women get tailbone pain more often. - People with a higher BMI, or who are very thin. See body weight and tailbone pain. - People who sit for long hours or ride over rough roads. See two-wheelers and tailbone pain. - People with some other conditions, such as ankylosing spondylitis or pelvic floor problems. See conditions linked to tailbone pain. High rates in particular groups Some studies have looked at specific groups of people. Their figures are much higher than the general rate, because these groups are exposed to particular risks. They should not be read as rates for a whole country. Group studied Share with tailbone pain Where and when Source People with ankylosing spondylitis 38.3% (vs 18.4% of women and 8% of men with ordinary back pain) Istanbul, Turkey, 2014; 107 patients Deniz 2014 Women seeking physiotherapy for pelvic pain 49.6% USA, 2022; 127 women Neville 2022 Male motorbike riders 33.2% Pakistan, 2025; 190 riders Fatima 2025 Long-term wheelchair users 76% South Punjab, Pakistan, 2024; 250 users Sanobar 2024 Tailbone pain in specific study groups. We have not found a published study measuring coccydynia across the general population of India. The two Pakistani studies are the closest regional data, and their settings (long sitting, motorbike commuting) are very familiar in Indian cities. How well does treatment work? Most people get better with simple measures: a cut-out cushion, changes to how and how long they sit, and hands-on treatment of the coccyx and pelvic floor muscles. Injections are an option if pain persists, and surgery is kept for a small, carefully selected group. See coccydynia treatment, step by step.

title: 8 ways to sit more comfortably with tailbone pain
summary: Desk job, long drives or a hard classroom bench? Small changes to how and how long you sit can take a lot of pressure off a sore coccyx.
text: If your tailbone hurts, sitting is usually the hardest part of the day. When you sit upright or lean back, part of your weight rests on the coccyx, the small bone at the very bottom of the spine. When it is bruised, inflamed or moving abnormally, that pressure turns into pain, and getting up from a chair can bring a sharp jolt. How you sit makes a real difference. These are the changes our patients find most useful. 1. Lean slightly forward Tilting your upper body a little forward shifts your weight onto your thigh bones and the "sitting bones" of your pelvis, and off the coccyx. Sitting on the front half of the chair with your feet flat on the floor makes this easier. 2. Use a cut-out cushion A wedge or U-shaped cushion with a gap at the back lets the tailbone hang free instead of pressing on the seat. Round "doughnut" rings help some people but can still press on the coccyx, so a cushion with an open back is usually better. Take it with you: to the office, the car and restaurants. What Dr Rajveer Singh looks for in a tailbone cushion: Feature Why it matters A cut-out or notch at the back The tailbone doesn't touch the seat at all Thicker at the back, thinner at the front Lifts the pelvis and tips your weight forward onto the thighs Firm foam, not soft memory foam You don't sink down until the coccyx touches the chair again Choosing a tailbone cushion. An ordinary soft pillow doesn't take the pressure off. 3. Choose firm seats over soft sofas It sounds backwards, but deep, soft sofas let you sink and roll back onto the tailbone. A firm, supportive chair with a cushion is kinder. 4. Get up every 30 minutes Pressure and stiffness build the longer you sit. Set a reminder to stand, walk a few steps or do a gentle stretch every half hour. On long drives, plan short breaks. 5. Stand up the smart way Shift forward to the edge of the seat, bring your feet back under you, and push up through your legs while keeping your back straight. This avoids rocking back onto the coccyx at the moment you rise. 6. Support your lower back A small cushion or rolled towel behind the lower back keeps you upright and stops you slumping, which tips weight back onto the tailbone. 7. Heat or ice For a few minutes at a time, a warm pack can relax tight muscles around the coccyx, and an ice pack wrapped in a cloth can calm a flare-up. Use whichever helps you more. 8. Keep your bowels comfortable Straining often makes tailbone pain worse. Plenty of water, fruit, vegetables and fibre help. If bowel movements are painful, ask your doctor or pharmacist about a gentle stool softener. When self-care isn't enough Most tailbone pain settles with time and sensible habits. If yours hasn't improved after a few weeks, keeps coming back, or stops you working or sleeping, it is worth having the coccyx and surrounding muscles properly examined. A displaced or stiff coccyx, or tight pelvic-floor muscles, often needs hands-on treatment rather than more waiting. See a doctor promptly if the pain comes with fever, numbness, leg weakness, or problems controlling your bladder or bowels.

title: Tailbone pain after having a baby
summary: Many new mothers find that sitting to feed their baby is surprisingly painful. Here is why childbirth can affect the coccyx, and how it is treated.
text: Tailbone pain is much more common in women than in men, and pregnancy and childbirth are among the main reasons. Many mothers notice it in the weeks after delivery, often while sitting to feed the baby, which is exactly when sitting is hardest to avoid. Why pregnancy and childbirth affect the coccyx - Hormones loosen the joints. During pregnancy, hormones relax the ligaments of the pelvis so the baby can pass through. The joint between the sacrum and the coccyx loosens too. - The baby's head presses on the coccyx during a vaginal delivery, pushing it backwards. Occasionally the coccyx is bruised, strained or even displaced. - Weight and posture change. Through pregnancy, the way you sit and stand changes, putting new strain on the lower spine and pelvic floor. - Assisted or long deliveries and larger babies make injury a little more likely. What it typically feels like - An ache or sharp pain right at the base of the spine - Worse when sitting, especially leaning back, and when standing up - Sometimes painful bowel movements or discomfort during intercourse What helps 1. A cut-out (wedge or U-shaped) cushion for feeding and for the car. 2. Feeding positions that take weight off the tailbone: lying on your side, or sitting leaning slightly forward with good back support. 3. Gentle pelvic-floor exercises once your midwife or doctor says it is safe. 4. Keeping stools soft: fluids and fibre, and avoiding straining. 5. Heat or cold packs for short periods. Before taking pain relief while breastfeeding, check with your doctor or pharmacist which medicines are suitable. When to get it checked Postnatal tailbone pain often eases over a few weeks, and in Dr Rajveer Singh's experience most of it settles within 3 to 4 months of delivery. If it is still there after about 4 months, keeps returning, or makes caring for your baby difficult, ask for an examination: the coccyx may have been pushed inward or outward during labour (see tailbone subluxation). When the coccyx has been pushed out of its normal position or the surrounding muscles stay in spasm, hands-on treatment can help a great deal, and you don't need to "just put up with it". See a doctor urgently if you have fever, a wound or swelling near the tailbone, numbness, or new problems with bladder or bowel control.

title: When tailbone pain needs urgent attention
summary: Most tailbone pain is mechanical and treatable without surgery. A few warning signs, though, mean you should see a doctor quickly. Here is what they are.
text: The vast majority of tailbone pain comes from a fall, childbirth, long sitting or strain on the coccyx and the muscles around it. It is uncomfortable and can be stubborn, but it isn't dangerous. Rarely, though, pain at the base of the spine is a sign of something that needs prompt medical care. See a doctor promptly if you have tailbone pain with: - Fever, chills or feeling generally unwell. This could mean an infection, such as an abscess or an infected cyst near the tailbone (a pilonidal cyst). - A lump, swelling, redness or a wound near the tailbone. - Unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer. Very occasionally, a growth in or near the sacrum or coccyx causes pain. - Pain that is severe and getting steadily worse, or pain that is just as bad lying down at night. - Pain after a major accident such as a road traffic collision or a fall from height, where a fracture is possible. Go to an emergency department straight away if you have: - Numbness around the buttocks, genitals or inner thighs (sometimes called "saddle" numbness) - New difficulty passing urine, or loss of bladder or bowel control - Weakness in one or both legs These can be signs of pressure on the nerves at the bottom of the spinal canal, which needs urgent assessment. Why a proper examination matters Because so many conditions can cause pain low in the back and pelvis, a specialist first takes a careful history and examines the coccyx, the joints around it and the pelvic muscles. When needed, X-rays taken sitting and standing can show whether the coccyx moves abnormally, and an MRI can rule out other causes. Only once the cause is clear should treatment begin. If none of the warning signs above apply, tailbone pain is usually treatable with self-care and targeted, hands-on therapy. Surgery is rarely needed.

title: What happens at a coccydynia consultation (and how to prepare)
summary: Nervous about your first visit for tailbone pain? Here is what to expect, step by step, and how to prepare so you get the most from the appointment.
text: Many people put off getting tailbone pain checked because they aren't sure what the visit involves, or they feel embarrassed. Knowing what happens makes it much easier. Before you come - Make a list of your medicines and any past operations or injuries. - Note how your pain behaves: when it started, what makes it worse (sitting, getting up, driving, bowel movements) and what helps. - Wear comfortable clothes. - If you would prefer to be seen by a female clinician , mention it when booking. 1. Listening and history The visit starts with a conversation: how the pain began (a fall, childbirth, long sitting or no clear reason), how long you have had it, how it affects your work, sleep and daily life, and what you have already tried. 2. Examination The clinician examines your lower back, pelvis and the area around the tailbone, checking for tenderness, swelling and how the coccyx and surrounding muscles respond to pressure and movement. Everything is explained first, and nothing happens without your consent. You can ask to pause at any time. 3. Pinpointing the cause The aim is to find out what is actually causing the pain: whether the coccyx is moving too much, too little or sitting out of position, whether the pelvic-floor muscles are in spasm, or whether something else needs ruling out. 4. Treatment plan You'll leave with a clear plan. Depending on the cause, this may include hands-on treatment such as manipulation of the coccyx and its muscles, together with posture and seating advice, a suitable cushion, and exercises you can do at home. Many patients notice a difference early, but the plan is always tailored to your own situation. 5. Follow-up After treatment, a short check-in a week or two later helps track your pain and sitting tolerance, so the plan can be adjusted if needed.
